The post Mayo Clinic Minute: Surgical advances help preserve function after stomach cancer treatment appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> Stomach cancer, also called gastric cancer, begins when cells grow abnormally in the stomach. More than 30,000 people in the U.S. are diagnosed with stomach cancer each year.
When stomach cancer is found early and has not spread, treatment can sometimes cure it. For cancer that has grown through the stomach wall or spread to other parts of the body, treatments may focus on controlling the cancer, relieving symptoms and helping people live longer.
In this Mayo Clinic Minute, Dr. Travis Grotz, a surgical oncologist at Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center, explains how surgical innovations can help patients preserve stomach function and quality of life.
Watch: The Mayo Clinic Minute
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (1:07) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
What happens during stomach cancer surgery?
Treatment depends on where the cancer is located in the stomach and its stage. Options may include chemotherapy, radiation therapy, targeted therapy, immunotherapy and surgery.
"Surgery involves removing all or part of the stomach, and that depends on the extent of the tumor in the stomach and the lymph nodes around the stomach," says Dr. Grotz.
The goal of surgery is to remove all the cancer. In some cases, that means removing the entire stomach in a procedure called a total gastrectomy. The surgeon then connects the esophagus to the small intestine so food can move through the digestive system.
"If patients need a total gastrectomy, what they've lost is their storage reservoir, so they're limited to eating very, very small meals frequently," says Dr. Grotz. "But what we can do is, we can recreate a new stomach out of their intestine. We call that a J-pouch, and that restores some of that capacity for patients to eat larger meals afterward. And so then when they recover, they can have more normal function in eating than if they didn't have that pouch."
For stomach cancer surgery, a J-pouch is made from the jejunum, a portion of the small intestine, and is therefore referred to as a jejunal J-pouch. The J-pouch technique is more commonly used in colorectal surgery, where a pouch similarly serves as a storage reservoir. With a jejunal J-pouch reconstruction after total gastrectomy, the surgeon folds a segment of jejunum into a J shape and connects it to itself, creating a larger reservoir before connecting it to the esophagus.
"Although less commonly used in stomach cancer surgery and technically demanding, at Mayo Clinic we routinely perform this specialized reconstruction, offering an additional option to select patients," says Dr. Grotz.
Can part of the stomach be preserved?
Mayo Clinic surgeons are also studying techniques that can preserve part of the stomach.
In many Western countries, including the U.S., stomach cancer often starts in the upper part of the stomach, near the esophagus, and may be more advanced when diagnosed.
"For a long time, we have saved the upper part of the stomach whenever there's a tumor in the lower part, but it's been more challenging to remove the upper part of the stomach and save the bottom," explains Dr. Grotz. "We adapted a surgical technique and have a lot of experience here at Mayo Clinic in removing all the cancer and saving that bottom part of the stomach to get the benefits of stomach preservation."

The post Mayo Clinic Minute: Robotic Whipple procedure for pancreatic cancer appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> Pancreatic cancer is one of the deadliest forms of cancer, in part because it often is diagnosed at an advanced stage. For some patients, treatment may include a complex surgery known as the Whipple procedure.
The Whipple procedure, also called a pancreaticoduodenectomy, is most commonly used to treat cancers located in the head of the pancreas.
Watch: The Mayo Clinic Minute
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (1:03) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
"The Whipple operation is commonly performed for cancer in the pancreatic head, and it involves removing the head of the pancreas along with part of the intestines surrounding it," says Dr. Zhi Ven Fong, a Mayo Clinic surgical oncologist and hepatobiliary and pancreas surgeon.
Historically, the procedure has been performed through a large abdominal incision. For some patients, surgeons can perform robotic-assisted Whipple procedures through several smaller incisions.
"Patients have smaller incisions; they have less pain after the operations. Their recovery is more expeditious as well," Dr. Fong says.
Pancreatic cancer treatment takes a team
Surgery is only one part of treatment for many people with pancreatic cancer. Dr. Fong says patients may receive a combination of treatments, including chemotherapy and surgery, depending on their individual circumstances.
"If we can get patients through what we call multimodal treatment, where they receive chemotherapy successfully, tolerate it well, get them to an operation, then that gives them the best shot at cure," he says.
Dr. Zhi Ven Fong and surgical team performing a robotic Whipple procedure.
Coordinating those treatments requires specialists from multiple areas working together throughout a patient's care.
"Our strength really is in the multidisciplinary team that we have," Dr. Fong says. "It's all about the collaborative team model to get a patient through multimodal treatment."
Join the conversation at the Mayo Clinic Connect Pancreatic Cancer Support Group.

Flip on the TV, and you're bound to find shows of horror, mystery and the macabre. Many people love the thrill of terror as suspense builds during a scary movie. These flicks can make your heart pound harder and eyes widen. The question is: Why does your body react when you know that what you're watching is not real? Dr. Regis Fernandes, a Mayo Clinic cardiologist, has some answers.
Watch: The Mayo Clinic Minute
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video pkg (0:59) is in the downloads at the end of the post.
Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
Scary movies. The dread, fear and horror that makes your pulse quicken and palms sweat.
Why does fear make your heart race?
"What happens to the human body when you watch a scary movie ... comes from the known fight or flight response. … When we are being chased by an animal, our instinct is to either fight the animal or flight, which means to run away," Dr. Fernandes says. "So, probably, that same mechanism gets triggered when we get scared by watching situations on the screen that are similar to that situation in real life."
Dr. Fernandes says three things happen: Your heart rate increases, blood flow to muscles increases and adrenaline flows.
"It’s similar to exercise," he says.
Are scary movies bad for your heart?
Dr. Fernandes does not suggest replacing exercise with watching scary movies, but he says that the body's reaction to being frightened is unlikely to hurt healthy individuals.
"If you enjoy that thrill, it’s not dangerous," Dr. Fernandes says.
And it seems many of us just love the feeling of being terrified.
Feeling stressed after a scary flick? Check out these tips to tame stress.

The post Mayo Clinic Minute: Unlocking how the liver regenerates after surgery (VIDEO) appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> The liver is the body's largest internal organ, helping to digest food, remove waste and make proteins. It's essential for life.
When part of the liver is removed to treat cancer or other conditions, the remaining tissue must regenerate to restore liver function.
In this Mayo Clinic Minute, Dr. Patrick Starlinger, a hepatobiliary and pancreas surgeon at Mayo Clinic Comprehensive Cancer Center, discusses research to help the liver regenerate after surgery.
Watch: The Mayo Clinic Minute
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (1:07) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
How does the liver regenerate after surgery?
"The liver can regenerate quite dramatically, probably the most potential to regenerate in the entire human body, and we leverage this in liver surgery," says Dr. Starlinger.
Before surgery, the team measures liver volume and assesses liver function to determine how much can be safely removed to take out the tumor while leaving enough healthy liver to regenerate.
But in some patients, that regeneration does not happen, which can lead to liver failure and limit which tumors can be removed.
"Our area of research is so important to understand the mechanism of liver regeneration in humans, particularly because as we understand the mechanism, we can move forward with interventions to promote regeneration in these patients," says Dr. Starlinger.
What role does blood clotting play in liver regeneration?
Mayo Clinic researchers have analyzed liver samples from patients with healthy livers and those with underlying liver conditions to better understand what drives regeneration.
"We were able to discover that the blood coagulation system is crucially important to allow these mechanisms of liver regeneration to actually occur," says Dr. Starlinger.
More research is needed, but researchers hope these findings could eventually lead to treatments that promote liver regeneration and expand the limits of liver surgery.

The post Mayo Clinic Minute: 3D printing brings a personalized fit to spine surgery (VIDEO) appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> No two spines are exactly alike, and personalized 3D-printed titanium options are giving Mayo Clinic surgeons a way to more closely match an implant to a patient's individual anatomy.
Instead of traditional implants manufactured in standard sizes, surgeons are using implants designed from a patient's own imaging.
"The benefit of these is they're custom fitted for each particular patient," says Dr. Joshua Bakhsheshian, a Mayo Clinic neurosurgeon. "This gives us a little bit more control in terms of alignment restoration and also (vertebral) endplate coverage, which leads to better patient outcomes down the line."
Watch: The Mayo Clinic Minute
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (1:00) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
Personalized implants, personalized care
Creating the implant starts with a CT scan. Resulting images are used to build a three-dimensional reconstruction of the patient's spine. From that reconstruction, an implant can be designed to fit the space between the vertebrae where it will be placed.
This personalized fit is part of an evolution in spine surgery toward better tailored treatments.
"Modern-day spine surgery requires a lot of planning beforehand," Dr. Bakhsheshian says. "The operation is mostly done before you even get to the operating room."
For patients undergoing spinal fusion, implants help maintain the space between vertebrae while the bones heal together. Porous titanium also allows bone to grow into and integrate better with the implant.
Better outcomes through customization
Dr. Bakhsheshian says customization can also mean less adjustment to the implant during the operation.
"They're personalized to each patient, which allows me to finish the operation quicker because there's less 'carpentry' that's needed in the operating room," he says.
This level of precision can also benefit patients after surgery.
"Patients tend to recover faster, and they're able to return to their level of activity as desired sooner," Dr. Bakhsheshian says.
A spinal implant may be small, but its role in supporting alignment, stability and healing is important.
"I'm very excited about this technology," Dr. Bakhsheshian says. "Ultimately, it can help provide better outcomes."

The post Mayo Clinic Minute: Early screening and treatment advances improve prostate cancer outcomes appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men, and finding it early can expand treatment options, including highly precise radiation that targets the tumor while protecting nearby tissue.
Watch: The Mayo Clinic Minute
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (1:00) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
Screening for prostate cancer can start with a blood test. A prostate-specific antigen, or PSA, test measures a protein produced by the prostate. An elevated level may indicate the need for further evaluation.
"Screening is important because the earlier you catch prostate cancer, the higher the likelihood of cure," says Dr. Albert Attia, a Mayo Clinic radiation oncologist.
Knowing when to begin screening is an important conversation to have with your healthcare team.
"Screening is recommended for men at the age of 50, and some data indicate it's better to get screened even at age 45, especially if you have a family history of prostate cancer," Dr. Attia says.
There are several treatment options when it comes to prostate cancer. Surgery, hormone therapy, radiation or a combination of those may be used.
One radiation option is intensity-modulated radiation therapy, or IMRT. The goal is to precisely target the tumor while limiting radiation to nearby tissue.
"This is a way for us to shape the dose of radiation to deliver the high dose areas to the tumor and avoid any critical structures nearby," says Dr. Attia. "We're able to achieve submillimeter accuracy."
Join the conversation at the Mayo Clinic Connect Prostate Cancer Support Group.

The post Mayo Clinic Minute: Seeing glioblastoma more clearly could improve how it’s treated appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> What doctors can't see can make glioblastoma especially difficult to treat.
This aggressive brain cancer can extend beyond what's visible on a standard MRI, making it difficult to precisely target treatment. Just 5% to 7% of patients survive five years after diagnosis.
Mayo Clinic researchers are studying advanced imaging techniques designed to bring more of the tumor into view and potentially give care teams a better-defined target.
"We're trying to develop and improve treatments that will help extend the length of time patients live, as well as their quality of life and function while they're alive," says Dr. William Breen, a radiation oncologist at Mayo Clinic. "From a radiation perspective, we need to be able to accurately see the tumor to accurately target it and treat it as well as possible."
Watch: The Mayo Clinic Minute
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (1:04) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
Seeing tumors more clearly
A standard MRI with contrast shows doctors where glioblastoma appears to be, but tumor cells can extend into the surrounding brain beyond what is clearly visible.
"In over half of patients, we find a tumor more than a centimeter beyond the standard MRI-defined tumor, and in 20% of patients, we find a tumor more than 2 centimeters beyond the standard MRI-identified tumor," Dr. Breen says.
To see more, Mayo Clinic investigators are combining advanced MRI techniques with research PET scans. The scans provide different clues, such as areas where cells are especially dense, where blood flow is increased or where there may be more aggressive tumor activity.
Together, they can give doctors a more detailed picture of the tumor and where it may extend.
Treating tumors more precisely and effectively
Because glioblastoma can extend beyond what doctors see on a traditional MRI, radiation treatment generally includes an extra margin around the visible tumor to help cover cancer cells that may be hidden.
Advanced imaging could help doctors more accurately identify those areas and tailor radiation accordingly. For some patients, that could mean treating a smaller area of the brain and reducing radiation exposure to healthy tissue.
"By using advanced imaging, we're able to treat a smaller area in many patients and reduce the amount of normal brain receiving radiation, which may make for a safer and better treatment," Dr. Breen says.
Researchers also are studying whether they can direct more intensive treatment toward areas that advanced imaging identifies as particularly concerning.
Greater precision may make it possible to give a higher dose of radiation at each treatment and finish therapy sooner. Dr. Breen says treatment has been shortened from three to six weeks to one to two weeks for some patients, meaning fewer trips to the hospital and more time at home.
Bringing specialties together
The research brings together experts across Mayo Clinic, including neurosurgeons, radiation oncologists, neuro-oncologists, neuroradiologists and nuclear medicine specialists.
"I think our strength at Mayo Clinic for treating glioblastoma is the multidisciplinary team," Dr. Breen says.
While glioblastoma remains challenging to treat, advances in imaging, surgery, radiation, chemotherapy and other therapies are helping researchers continue to improve care.
"We know there's still much progress to be made," Dr. Breen says, "but we have seen progress over the years to improve both quality of life and quantity of life for our patients with glioblastomas."

The post Mayo Clinic Minute: Understanding brain aneurysms and treatment options (VIDEO) appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> September is Brain Aneurysm Awareness Month, a time to learn more about a condition that can develop without noticeable symptoms. In the U.S., approximately 1 in 50 people may have an unruptured brain aneurysm. Understanding the condition and when treatment may be needed can be lifesaving.
A brain aneurysm, also called a cerebral aneurysm, is a bulge or ballooning in a blood vessel in the brain. Aneurysms generally fall into two categories: ruptured aneurysms, which are neurosurgical emergencies requiring immediate care, and unruptured aneurysms, which allow time to evaluate treatment and monitoring options.
Watch: The Mayo Clinic Minute
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video pkg (0:56) is in the downloads at the end of the post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
"For unruptured aneurysms, we have the ability to plan and make a decision on the best treatment upfront in a nonemergent situation," says Dr. Chris Fox, a Mayo Clinic neurosurgeon.
But when a brain aneurysm ruptures, prompt medical attention is required.
"Typically, when we see a patient with a ruptured aneurysm, we treat it as quickly as possible. That's usually within a matter of hours because there's a risk that the aneurysm can rerupture," he says.
Symptoms of a ruptured aneurysm can include severe head pain, nausea, vomiting, confusion and loss of consciousness.
"The classic presentation for a ruptured aneurysm is a patient has the worst headache of their life," Dr. Fox says.
Brain aneurysms are more common in women, and there may be a genetic component because aneurysms can run in families.
"But smoking and hypertension are two of the biggest risk factors for causing an aneurysm or having an aneurysm form," says Dr. Fox.

Endometrial cancer begins in the endometrium, the lining of the uterus.
"We are seeing an increase in patients under the age of 45, where particularly our patients who may be in their 20s or 30s and still want future fertility," says Dr. Evelyn Reynolds, a Mayo Clinic gynecologic oncologist.
Standard treatment for endometrial cancer is a hysterectomy, a surgery to remove the uterus. But for some younger patients who want to preserve their ability to become pregnant, there may be another option.
"There are certain criteria that, if a patient meets, they may be a good candidate for fertility-sparing treatment," says Dr. Reynolds. "Lower-grade tumors that are confined to the endometrium are the ideal ones for treatment that can spare the uterus. There are different ways in which we can do targeted resection of the tumor."
Which is bringing hope to eligible patients who want to have children in the future.
"We don't make assumptions. It's always a conversation with the patients, and it's a multidisciplinary approach," says Dr. Reynolds. "I want them to know that there are options."

The post Mayo Clinic Minute: Leukemia isn’t like other cancers (VIDEO) appeared first on Mayo Clinic News Network. ]]> September is Blood Cancer Awareness Month. This year alone, nearly 68,000 people in the U.S. will be diagnosed with leukemia. Mayo Clinic hematologist and oncologist Dr. Cecilia Arana Yi says treatment is changing, and it's giving patients more options.
Watch: the Mayo Clinic Minute
Journalists: Broadcast-quality video (1:09) is in the downloads at the end of this post. Please courtesy: "Mayo Clinic News Network." Read the script.
Unlike many cancers that form solid tumors, leukemia is a cancer of the blood-forming cells in the bone marrow.
Dr. Arana Yi says, "Leukemia affects the production of the blood cells and can circulate through all the body from the beginning."
Leukemia isn't a single disease. There are several types that can behave differently. According to Dr. Arana Yi, "It is a group of cancers with different subtypes. Some develop very quickly, while others progress slowly."
Leukemia can affect people of all ages. Symptoms can include persistent fatigue, unusual bruising or bleeding, frequent infections, fever, night sweats, unexplained weight loss and shortness of breath.
"If those are persistent, it is important to review and be evaluated by a doctor for a possibility of a blood count checkup," Dr. Arana Yi mentions.
Research is helping doctors identify genetic changes that may be driving a patient's leukemia. That information can help guide treatment.
Dr. Arana Yi says, "This allows us to use targeted medicines, immune-based therapies, sometimes with less traditional chemotherapy or chemo-free regimen."
Recognizing possible symptoms and seeking medical evaluation can help doctors diagnose leukemia and determine appropriate treatment.
